title: About
text:
This is my coursework portfolio for Geospatial Analytics and Applications, part of the Master of IT in Business programme at Singapore Management University.
Everything on this site is built with Quarto and R. The main packages I work with are sf for handling spatial objects, tmap for thematic mapping, spdep and sfdep for spatial weights and autocorrelation, spatstat for point pattern analysis, and GWmodel for geographically weighted regression.

title: About
text:
A note on reproducibility
Each page shows the code that produced every figure and table. Where a dataset is small enough, it is stored alongside the analysis in this repository. Where it is not, the source and the download steps are documented at the top of the page so that the work can be repeated from scratch.
I use Quarto’s freeze feature, which caches computed results and only re-executes a page when its source changes. This keeps the site fast to rebuild, but it also means the committed output reflects the last successful run rather than a fresh run on every deploy.

title: About
text:
Projections
All analysis in this portfolio uses SVY21 (EPSG:3414) as the projected coordinate reference system. Singapore geospatial data arrives in a mixture of SVY21 and WGS84 (EPSG:4326), and any calculation involving distance, area, or spatial weights requires a projected CRS rather than a geographic one. Where a dataset needs converting, the transformation step is shown explicitly rather than assumed.

title: Hands-on Exercise 01: Geospatial Data Wrangling
text:
Checking the coordinate reference system
Always confirm the CRS before doing anything else. Singapore data arrives in a mix of SVY21 and WGS84, and any calculation involving distance or area needs a projected CRS.

st_crs(mpsz)


mpsz3414 <- st_transform(mpsz, crs = 3414)







NoteNote to self



st_set_crs() and st_transform() do different things. st_set_crs() only relabels the data as being in a given CRS without moving any coordinates, so it is the right tool when the CRS tag is wrong but the numbers are fine. st_transform() actually reprojects the coordinates. Using the first when I meant the second silently produces wrong distances.

title: Geospatial Analytics and Applications
text:
Meng Tingyu


Master of IT in Business, Singapore Management University
This is where I keep my work for Geospatial Analytics and Applications. Over the term it will fill up with weekly exercises and three larger take-home analyses, covering geospatial data wrangling, thematic mapping, spatial point patterns, spatial autocorrelation, clustering, and geographically weighted models.
Everything here is written in R and Quarto, and the code that produced each figure is visible on the page. I work this way for a practical reason. When an analysis is written up properly, I find out fairly quickly whether I understand the method or only know which function to call, and that gap is much cheaper to discover here than in an exam.
A word on what I am aiming for. Geospatial work makes it unusually easy to produce something that looks convincing and is quietly wrong. A map with the wrong projection still renders. A spatial weights matrix built on the wrong neighbour definition still returns a Moran’s I. So alongside the results, I try to record the assumptions each method needs and the checks I ran before trusting the output.
